vignette:
At twenty-nine, he works with his hands all day, setting tiny stones into delicate bands, repairing broken clasps, leaning over a bench under a white task lamp until the rest of the room fades out. Customers know him as patient and precise. They do not see how hard-won that steadiness is, or how often his mind slips back to another place where his hands also worked nonstop, but nothing stayed fixed.

A few years earlier, he signs on as a relief worker and is sent into a war zone with an international aid group. He tells himself he is useful there. He helps unload medical supplies, organizes water distribution, carries children too weak to walk, translates where he can, and learns quickly how to move when shelling starts. At first he runs on urgency and adrenaline. Everyone around him is exhausted, frightened, determined. The days are chaotic but simple in their purpose: keep going, help the next person, make it through the night.

The event he returns to most often happens near the end of his deployment. A distribution point has formed outside a damaged school building. Families are already lined up when the first blast lands nearby. He remembers the sound less as a bang than as a violent pressure in his chest, as if the air itself turns solid. Then dust, screaming, the smell of burning fuel, people running in every direction. He drops to the ground, then gets up because others are getting up and because someone is shouting for stretchers. He sees a boy in a red sweater pinned beneath broken concrete. He and another worker try to free him while more explosions sound in the distance. He remembers the boy's face clearly-alert, terrified, trying not to cry-and he remembers realizing, before anyone says it aloud, that they are too late. Even now, what returns to him is not only the image of the boy but the unbearable fact of his own movement in that moment: his hands tugging uselessly, his mind calculating, the part of him that has to leave one body and run toward the next injured person.

He comes home expecting, vaguely, that time and distance will sort things out. Instead, ordinary life feels fraudulent. At the jewelry shop, the bright cases and quiet music strike him as obscene at first. He startles at the buzz of the door, at dropped tools, at delivery trucks braking outside. When a polishing motor whines at a certain pitch, his whole body tightens before he can think. He begins scanning every room automatically, noting exits, heavy furniture, anyone who seems agitated. He sits with his back to the wall in cafés and avoids crowded places entirely if he can.

Sleep becomes the worst part of the day. He dreads it, then needs it desperately. When he does fall asleep, he is back at the schoolyard or in some variation of it-dust in his mouth, someone calling for help, his legs heavy and slow. He wakes soaked in sweat, sometimes halfway out of bed, heart pounding so hard he presses a hand to his chest. More than once he has swung his arm toward the lamp beside him before fully waking, as if clearing debris. After nights like that, he goes to work already exhausted, his eyes burning under the magnifier.

He does not talk much about the war. Friends ask broad, admiring questions-what was it like over there?-and he gives them careful, deadened answers. He notices their relief when he keeps it vague. Being single makes it easier to hide. No one is there to hear him pacing his apartment at 3 a.m. or to notice that he keeps bottled water, flashlights, extra batteries, and a packed duffel by the door. He tells himself he just likes to be prepared.

The guilt is constant and shape-shifting. Sometimes it attaches to the boy in the red sweater; sometimes to colleagues he has lost contact with; sometimes to the simple fact that he now spends an afternoon resetting an engagement diamond while people he knew are still living under bombardment. He feels ashamed of how bitter that can make him. A customer cries happily when she sees her repaired heirloom necklace and he smiles, says the right things, then feels hollow and cruel for inwardly thinking that none of this matters.

Concentration, once his pride, now frays under pressure. Jewelry work demands meticulous attention, and on good days the precision soothes him: file, solder, set, inspect. On bad days, his hands pause midair when an image breaks in uninvited. The flash of red wool. Gray dust coating eyelashes. A child's shoe lying by itself. He loses minutes staring through the bench pin, then jolts back with a surge of panic, afraid he has made an expensive mistake. He checks his work repeatedly, not because he doubts his skill but because his mind no longer feels fully under his command.

He is more irritable than he used to be. Small frustrations-an order entered wrong, a customer tapping the glass, a stranger standing too close behind him in line-send heat through him instantly. He rarely explodes, but he goes hard and silent, jaw clenched, shoulders rigid, until the feeling burns out. Afterwards he is embarrassed by the intensity of it and even more unsettled by how familiar it feels, like his body is still living in emergency conditions long after the emergency has passed.

What troubles him most in the present is how split his life feels. At his workbench, under the lamp, he can still make something fragile hold together. Outside that pool of light, the world feels unpredictable, loud, and morally disorienting. He wants connection, but he keeps people at a distance because he cannot bear their curiosity, their pity, or the possibility that he might finally tell the story in full and be back inside it completely. So he keeps showing up to the shop, steadying trembling fingers over gold and stone, while part of him remains in that shattered schoolyard, listening for the next blast.
